summary: Describes the Finger protocol, a simple way to ask a remote host's user information program about the people using it. A client connects and sends a short query, and the server replies with plain text about the user or the logged-in users.

eli5.summary: Finger is like knocking on a door and asking who is home. You type a name, and the other computer sends back a short note about that person.

questions: what is a ruip in finger
subtitle: A simple TCP protocol for asking a remote host about the people using it.

tldr.problem: People wanted a standard way to ask a remote computer who is logged in or to look up a specific user, but the original description of Finger was unclear and implementations differed.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 79 and sends a one-line query in ASCII. The remote user information program (RUIP) answers with human-readable text and closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: The memo clarifies the query grammar and adds extensive security advice, because Finger discloses sensitive information about users. It obsoletes RFCs 742, 1194 and 1196.

facts.label: Data format
facts.value: ASCII, no parity, lines end in CRLF

today: RFC 1288 is listed as a Draft Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaces RFC 742, RFC 1194 and RFC 1196.

sections.title: Intent and History
sections.content:
Finger is a simple protocol that gives an interface to a remote user information program (RUIP). The memo is based on RFC 742, the original Finger description, and tries to clarify what the two ends of a connection should do without invalidating existing implementations.

Most Finger implementations of the time derived from BSD UNIX, so the memo follows the BSD behavior. Because that version offers little control over what is revealed, the memo adds many security comments. It also records that the FINGER program at SAIL, by Les Earnest, inspired the NAME program on ITS.

Compared with RFC 1196, this edition moves the optional /W switch to the beginning of the query, makes the BNF explicit about blank space, and better defines how the connection is closed.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up rulebook for an old way of asking computers about their users, with extra warnings about privacy.

sections.title: How a Finger Connection Works
sections.content:
Finger runs over TCP using port 79 decimal (117 octal). The local host opens a connection to that port on the remote host, and an RUIP becomes available to handle the request. The local host sends a one-line query and waits. The RUIP processes the query, returns an answer and then starts the close of the connection. The local host receives the answer and the close, then closes its own end.

All data MUST be ASCII with no parity, and lines MUST end in CRLF. Bytes between ASCII 128 and 255 should be genuinely international data, not 7-bit ASCII with the parity bit set.
sections.eli5: You knock on a specific door (port 79), ask one question, get one answer, and the other side hangs up first.

sections.title: The Query Specification
sections.content:
An RUIP MUST accept the entire query specification, which has two forms. {Q1} is an optional /W (alone, or followed by spaces and a user name) and a CRLF. {Q2} is an optional /W and spaces, an optional user name, then one or more @hostname tokens and a CRLF. Because @hostname is recursive, there is no arbitrary limit on how many appear.

The forms describe the line the RUIP actually receives, not what a person types. If a user types finger user@host, the RUIP on the remote host receives user and a CRLF, which is a {Q1} query. The memo adds the usual advice to be liberal in what you accept.
sections.eli5: A query is a short sentence: maybe a name, maybe a list of computers to pass the question along through.

sections.title: Forwarding {Q2} Queries
sections.content:
A {Q2} query asks the RUIP to forward the question to another RUIP. An RUIP MUST either provide this service or actively refuse it. If it provides it, it takes the right-most host in the query as the next target, removes that @hostname token, and opens its own Finger connection to that host with the remaining query.

It must return everything it receives from that connection to the original client. In normal circumstances it MUST close the first connection only when the second host closes the second one.
sections.eli5: It is like passing a note down a row of desks. Each person hands it on to the next one and carries the answer back.

sections.title: What an RUIP Answers
sections.content:
Output is meant for people, so it has no strict format. It should mainly be informative, and all output is subject to the security rules.

  • An empty query {C} asks for all online users. The RUIP MUST answer with at least each user's full name, or actively refuse. Administrators SHOULD be able to add items such as terminal location, office location, office phone and idle time.
  • A user query {U}{C} asks for in-depth status of one user. The answer MUST include at least the full name, and at least as much as the online list for a logged-in user. A user information file (sometimes called a plan file) may be included.
  • If a name is ambiguous, administrators SHOULD be able to choose whether all matches are returned.
  • The /W token SHOULD at best be read by the last RUIP as a request for more verbose output, or at worst be ignored.

The memo also says vending machines SHOULD answer an empty query with the items available for purchase, and should never eat money.
sections.eli5: If you ask for everyone, you get a list. If you ask for one person, you get more detail, maybe even a note they left for visitors.

sections.title: Security Advice
sections.content:
The memo opens its security section with a warning: Finger discloses information about users, which may be sensitive. It says Finger was one avenue of direct penetration, as the Morris worm showed, and it sits at the security perimeter of a host like Telnet, FTP and SMTP. An RUIP SHOULD protect itself against malformed input.

For the server side, the memo asks for administrator controls:

  • Forwarding of {Q2} queries SHOULD be switchable, and if off the RUIP MUST return a refusal. The default is RECOMMENDED to be refusal, because forwarding provides a path through a security perimeter.
  • The online user list {C} SHOULD be switchable, and a refusal MUST be returned if it is off.
  • Administrators SHOULD choose which items of information are returned, down to the minimum of the full name.
  • User information files and running user programs are risky. The RUIP MUST NOT allow system security to be compromised by such a program.
  • Implementations SHOULD allow logging of queries.

On the client side, the program SHOULD by default filter output to printable characters ASCII 32 through 126, tabs and CRLFs, to guard against terminal escape codes.
sections.eli5: Because the answers tell strangers about real people, the owner of the computer should be able to choose what to share, or to say no.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The memo gives four sample sessions. An empty line returns a table of logged-in users with login, name, terminal, idle time, login time and office. A name such as pirmann returns that user's details and a plan. An ambiguous name such as ron returns several matching users. A query hedrick@math.rutgers.edu@pilot.njin.net is sent to dimacs.rutgers.edu and passes through pilot.njin.net and math.rutgers.edu, which each print their name in brackets before the result.
sections.eli5: The examples show what the replies look like: a list for everyone, a longer note for one person, and a chain through several computers.
